newsitem.title: UK: Global debt under threat if yen turns.
newsitem.headline: Global debt under threat if yen turns.

text.p: Global bond markets are in for a blow-out if recent yen weakness is halted and the dollar is sent scuttling lower, analysts said on Tuesday.

Comments by a Japanese Finance Ministry (MoF) official last week suggested Japan has had enough of seeing the yen falter against the dollar, and raised fears of a reversal in the trend taking the shine off recent bond market rallies.
"It would not necessarily be fatal, but it could cause quite a decent correction in global bond markets," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
Since April last year, when the dollar bottomed out at 79.70 yen, the U.S. currency has staged an impressive rally, reaching as high as 114.91 in the past few weeks.
Global bond investors have enjoyed the ride.
Borrowing in yen, where interest rates are just 0.5 percent, players have plunged into higher-yielding debt markets with the currency risk limited by Japanese enthusiasm for a weak yen.
But the yen can no longer be treated as a one-way bet.

Finance ministry Vice-Minister Eisuke Sakakibara, known to the markets as "Mr Yen", was quoted as saying last week that the Japanese economy was stronger than the market believed. The hour of the strong dollar was over, he said. While analysts said a sharp reversal in the dollar's rally was unlikely in the near term, they said investors should keep watch over the next 12 months.
European high yielding markets, such as Italy, Spain and Sweden, would be among the main victims if the dollar were to lose its footing.
These markets traditionally gain when the dollar is strong, since the mark is left in a weaker position and units such as the lira and peseta gain ground on European crosses.

Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, and Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said Australian and New Zealand bond markets were likely to suffer the most.
"Those are the ones which are most reliant on Japanese fund flows at the moment," Schmidt said.
Baader said Japanese investors, seeing rich rewards beginning to be wiped out by yen appreciation, would soon revert to domestic markets, pulling large capital flows out of overseas markets.

"If people see their positions under threat from an appreciation in the yen, and they have suspicions that the Japanese may consider raising overnight rates, that will lead them to reverse those trades," he said.
The dollar recovered from two-month lows against the mark on Tuesday and was quoted at 1.4940/45 in European midsession business. Against the yen it was at 111.35 by 1325 GMT.

A trigger for a more substantial move -- of a potentially destructive size for bond markets -- was unlikely to come for some time, analysts said, and could well be in the form of a monetary tightening in Japan in the first half of 1997.

"It is certainly clear that the Japanese MoF does not want the weaker yen trend to continue in the short term," said Chase's Schmidt. "But there is a long way to go from saying that to actually seeing dollar/yen move lower."
